title: Epicardial adipose tissue induces endothelial dysfunction via Activin A-mediated endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition and mitochondrial dysfunction.
summary: Patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) exhibit elevated risks of endothelial dysfunction, though the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. As a unique visceral adipose tissue, epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) may play a crucial role in regulating endothelial function and is significantly thickened in AF patients. However, the mechanism by which EAT influences endothelial dysfunction in AF patients has not been elucidated. In this study, we found that human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) treated with EAT-conditioned medium exhibited significantly elevated endothelial injury markers and increased expression of Activin A. Suppressing Activin A expression using shRNA partially alleviated endothelial dysfunction. Transcriptome sequencing analysis revealed that, compared to HUVECs treated with subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT)-conditioned medium, differentially expressed genes in HUVECs treated with EAT-conditioned medium were mainly enriched in pathways related to endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) and mitochondrial biogenesis and bioenergetics. Further investigation demonstrated that EAT-conditioned medium suppressed the expression of endothelial markers (VE-cadherin and CD31) in HUVECs while increasing the expression of mesenchymal markers (α-SMA and vimentin) and initiating the EndMT process by activating Smad2/3 binding to SNAIL. Additionally, the Seahorse assay showed that mitochondrial respiration was significantly inhibited in EAT-treated HUVECs, accompanied by impaired mitochondrial biogenesis pathways and upregulated oxidative stress. While suppressing Activin A expression using shRNA effectively ameliorated the detrimental effects of EAT on EndMT and mitochondrial function in HUVECs. Therefore, targeted inhibition of Activin A in endothelial cells may be a potential strategy for alleviating EAT-mediated endothelial dysfunction in AF patients.

title: Dual-channel surface-enhanced Raman immunoassay for simultaneous determination of atrial-fibrillation-associated NT-proBNP and high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I in artificial serum
summary: Atrial fibrillation is associated with myocardial wall stress and low-grade injury, yet parallel measurement of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) generally requires separate immunoassays. We developed a single-chamber, dual-channel surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) immunoassay that combines antibody-functionalised magnetic capture beads with Au@Ag nanotags encoded by 4-mercaptobenzonitrile at 2227 cm-1 and 4-mercaptobenzoic acid at 1077 cm-1. A 9 × 9 full-factorial calibration design spanning 0-10 000 pg per mL NT-proBNP and 0-500 pg per mL hs-cTnI was executed across three independently prepared tag lots. Ten spatial spectra were aggregated at the sample level, preprocessed and quantified by a batch-grouped partial least-squares model. Limits of detection were 6.30 pg mL-1 for NT-proBNP and 0.46 pg mL-1 for hs-cTnI; corresponding limits of quantification were 18.7 and 1.35 pg mL-1. Across matrix lots and concentration levels, recoveries were 93.1-107.8% and total coefficients of variation were 4.8-9.4%. Thirty-six independently prepared, blinded artificial-serum specimens representing four dual-biomarker phenotypes were compared with electrochemiluminescence and chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassays. Under an equal-error-variance assumption, Deming slopes were 0.963 and 1.012, concordance correlation coefficients were 0.9951 and 0.9930, and concentration-quadrant agreement was 35/36. Grouped validation and specimen-level comparison assessed the dual readout without treating spatial spectra as independent replicates. This architecture provides a controlled route to simultaneous cardiac-biomarker measurement in artificial serum.

title: From Presumed Post-Stroke Seizures to Probable Ventricular Tachycardia: Antiseizure Therapy, Diagnostic Misattribution and Human Oversight of Smartwatch ECGs-A Narrative Review.
summary: Transient arrhythmias can produce episodes that resemble seizures, and an incorrect attribution can lead to treatment that does not address the underlying mechanism. This narrative review is informed by the case of a patient with haemorrhagic stroke and severe left ventricular dysfunction whose recurrent episodes were considered compatible with epileptic seizures and treated with levetiracetam. Episodes recurred despite treatment. Smartwatch electrocardiograms (ECGs) obtained by relatives had been labelled inadequate and were understood to show no abnormality. On cardiologist review, one showed a regular wide-complex tachycardia interpreted as probable ventricular tachycardia; a single lead could not exclude supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction, and urgent tertiary assessment was advised. We discuss three connected issues. First, the clinical features and cardiac substrate that should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis when episodes persist despite antiseizure therapy. Second, evidence, largely from atrial fibrillation studies, that unclassified wearable recordings often remain interpretable by clinicians, and the more limited evidence for ventricular arrhythmias. Third, the conditions under which such recordings reach clinical review, including digital health literacy, communication of uncertainty, and services that receive recordings and communicate the plan. We propose assigning these responsibilities explicitly, including when artificial intelligence informs interpretation or triage. These arrangements require evaluation.

title: Biatrial Echocardiographic Remodeling and Atrial Fibrillation Recurrence in HFpEF/HFmrEF: A Prospective Cohort Study.
summary: Background/Objectives: Atrial fibrillation (AF) recurrence reflects a complex atrial remodeling substrate, but the relative associations of left atrial (LA) structural remodeling, deformation, and right atrial (RA) involvement remain uncertain. We investigated echocardiographic markers of biatrial remodeling in relation to AF recurrence in patients with HFpEF/HFmrEF. Methods: We prospectively studied 116 patients with paroxysmal or persistent AF and HFpEF/HFmrEF. Left atrial volume index (LAVI) and LA reservoir strain (LASr) represented LA structural and functional remodeling, while right atrial (RA) area was evaluated as a secondary biatrial marker. The primary endpoint was electrocardiographically documented AF recurrence within 365 days. Cause-specific Cox models adjusted for age, sex, and AF type. Results: Forty-nine patients experienced AF recurrence within 365 days. Higher LAVI was consistently associated with recurrence (HR 1.79 per 10 mL/m2, 95% CI 1.17-2.72; p = 0.007), whereas the average linear association of lower LASr was weaker (HR 1.25 per 5-percentage-point decrease, 95% CI 0.96-1.64; p = 0.093) and substantially overlapped with structural remodeling. The RA area was associated with AF recurrence when evaluated individually, but its incremental contribution beyond LA remodeling was less consistent, and its association varied over time. Internal validation demonstrated modest discrimination, with little improvement from increasing model complexity. Conclusions: In patients with AF and HFpEF/HFmrEF, atrial structural and functional remodeling showed overlapping associations with AF recurrence. LAVI provided the most consistent echocardiographic signal, whereas LASr conveyed partly overlapping and more complex information. RA findings were exploratory and require confirmation in larger cohorts. These results support further investigation of biatrial remodeling while cautioning against individualized recurrence prediction from these markers alone.

title: Mitochondrial Calcium Response Mismatch in Metabolic Atrial Fibrillation: A Proposed Mechanistic Framework Linking Metabolic Stress to Atrial Fibrillation Vulnerability, Burden, and Recurrence.
summary: Obesity and metabolic syndrome are increasingly recognized as major drivers of atrial fibrillation (AF), and patients with this phenotype commonly exhibit a higher AF burden, more rapid progression from paroxysmal to persistent disease, and an increased risk of recurrence after catheter ablation. Conventional explanations, including structural remodeling, inflammation, and electrophysiological heterogeneity, account for part of this phenotype but do not fully explain why metabolic AF is often less responsive to conventional rhythm-control strategies. Here, we discuss that workload-inappropriate mitochondrial calcium responsiveness represents a candidate intermediate phenotype linking metabolic stress to atrial arrhythmogenesis. Under physiological conditions, mitochondrial calcium uptake couples excitation to energy production by synchronizing ATP generation, redox buffering, and ion homeostasis with beat-to-beat calcium cycling. In the metabolically stressed atrium, however, lipotoxicity, substrate inflexibility, oxidative stress, chronic low-grade inflammation, and disruption of sarcoplasmic reticulum-mitochondrial microdomains may impair or destabilize workload-responsive mitochondrial Ca2+ handling. This may create a state of energy-calcium mismatch in which atrial excitation is no longer matched by adequate metabolic support. The downstream consequences are predicted to include ATP insufficiency, impaired calcium reuptake, sodium-calcium disequilibrium, reactive oxygen species amplification, reduced stress tolerance, and progressive structural remodeling, together creating both triggers and substrate for AF. We further discuss how this framework can be tested through functional readouts, such as mitochondrial respiratory reserve, NAD(P)H/FAD redox recovery, redox stress markers, mitochondrial and cytosolic Ca2+ dynamics, and circulating mitochondrial injury signals, and how these measures may align with clinically relevant endpoints including AF burden and post-ablation recurrence. The model may be particularly relevant in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), in whom metabolic overload, inflammation, microvascular dysfunction, impaired oxygen delivery, and atrial pressure stress converge and may reduce atrial metabolic reserve; however, direct evidence that HFpEF represents an atrial mitochondrial Ca2+-mismatch phenotype remains limited. Taken together, this electro-metabolic framework provides a testable mechanistic model for metabolic AF and generates clinically relevant predictions that require prospective validation.

title: One-Stop Catheter Ablation Combined With "Kissing" Left Atrial Appendage Closure in a Patient With Dextrocardia and Atrial Fibrillation: A Case Report.
summary: One-stop catheter ablation (CA) combined with left atrial appendage (LAA) closure (LAAC) is widely used in patients with atrial fibrillation (AFib); however, it is extremely challenging to perform catheter-based procedures in rare cases of AFib with dextrocardia and complex LAA anatomy. Such cases may require precise occlusion strategies, such as dual-device "Kissing LAAC." However, to our knowledge, no cases of one-stop CA combined with Kissing LAAC in patients with AFib, dextrocardia, and complex LAA anatomy have been reported. A 67-year-old woman with persistent AFib and dextrocardia was found on preoperative computed tomography angiography (CTA) to have a complex bilobed LAA with a shared orifice diameter of approximately 26 mm and shared depth of approximately 12 mm. Therefore, single-device closure was considered unlikely to achieve effective occlusion. A one-stop CA combined with LAAC procedure was planned. After CA, intraoperative multi-projection digital subtraction angiography (DSA) was used to determine the deployment angle, evaluate the superior and inferior lobes, and guide device selection. Two 20-mm WATCHMAN FLX devices were implanted under DSA guidance, and the procedure was completed without immediate complications. At the 3-month follow-up, the patient maintained sinus rhythm, and CTA showed stable device position without device-related thrombus. However, a residual shunt of 2.92 mm was observed on 3-month CTA. This case suggests that one-stop CA combined with Kissing LAAC may be technically feasible in a highly selected patient with AFib, dextrocardia, and complex bilobed LAA anatomy, and it may provide a valuable clinical reference for similar cases.

title: Current Status and Future Prospects of Catheter Ablation for Brugada Syndrome
summary: Brugada syndrome is a type of arrhythmia with a highly hereditary tendency with characteristic electrocardiographic findings that is associated with lethal arrhythmias. An implantable cardioverter defibrillator is recommended to avoid cardiac sudden death, because medical therapy cannot completely suppress the occurrence of ventricular fibrillation (VF). Meanwhile, ablation for Brugada syndrome has been reported to prevent VF. The targets of ablation are the triggers of premature ventricular contraction that induce VF, and the substrate of the epicardium in the right ventricular outflow tract where VF may develop and be maintained. After substrate ablation, the characteristic electrocardiogram in Brugada syndrome normalizes, and VF is prevented in many patients. Based on the characteristics of the abnormal delayed potentials observed in the epicardial arrhythmogenic substrate, the target of ablation, although depolarization abnormalities are considered a possible mechanism underlying Brugada syndrome, it appears that repolarization abnormalities are also involved.

title: Impact of Body Mass Index on Recurrence After Catheter Ablation for Persistent Atrial Fibrillation in Patients With Left Atrial Low-Voltage Areas　- Prespecified Subanalysis of the SUPPRESS-AF Trial
summary: Background Low-voltage area ablation (LVA-ABL) is used for substrate modification in persistent atrial fibrillation (AF), but whether its benefit varies by body mass index (BMI) is uncertain.Methods and results This prespecified subanalysis of the multicenter randomized SUPPRESS-AF trial included patients with persistent AF undergoing initial catheter ablation. After pulmonary vein isolation (PVI), patients with low-voltage areas (LVAs; bipolar voltage <0.5 mV) totaling ≥5 cm2were randomized to adjunctive LVA-ABL or PVI alone. Overall, 341 patients were stratified by BMI quartile (Q1, 14.1-20.8 kg/m2; Q2, 20.9-23.3 kg/m2; Q3, 23.4-26.0 kg/m2; Q4, 26.1-37.9 kg/m2). The primary endpoint was AF/atrial tachycardia (AT) recurrence after a 3-month blanking period without antiarrhythmic drugs through 12 months. Overall AF/AT recurrence did not differ by BMI quartile (log-rank P=0.97). In BMI-stratified analyses, adjunctive LVA-ABL was associated with lower recurrence than PVI alone in Q2 (28.6% vs. 53.5%; log-rank P=0.020; adjusted hazard ratio 0.47; 95% confidence interval 0.22-0.95), whereas no clear benefit was observed in Q1, Q3, or Q4. The treatment-by-BMI interaction was not statistically significant (P=0.089).Conclusions Adjunctive LVA-ABL did not demonstrate a statistically significant treatment-by-BMI interaction. Although recurrence was lower in the BMI Q2, this subgroup finding should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis generating. Further studies are warranted to determine whether substrate burden can refine substrate definition and lesion targeting.

Mapping the Right Atrial Ganglionated Plexuses Using the Novel Tau20-RETROmapping System.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Ectopy-triggering ganglionated plexuses (ET-GPs) from the intrinsic cardiac autonomic nervous system are proposed upstream drivers of atrial fibrillation (AF). The investigational Tau20-RETROmapping system (TauRhythm Therapies, UK) was developed to identify ET-GPs and was used to characterize their distribution in the right atrium (RA) of patients undergoing repeat AF ablation.

OBJECTIVE: To characterize the anatomical distribution and nature of RA-GP sites using the Tau20-RETROmapping system.

METHODS: Patients undergoing re-do AF ablation were recruited. The Tau20-RETROmapping system was used to map RA ET-GP sites by delivering synchronized high-frequency stimulation (HFS; 50 mA, 40 Hz, 80 ms, up to 15 trains) via a contact-force-sensing ablation catheter. If sinus rhythm could not be maintained, AV-dissociating-GP (AVD-GP) sites were identified using continuous HFS (50 mA, 20 Hz, 10 s). All test sites were annotated on a 3D electroanatomic map.

RESULTS: 54 patients underwent RA-GP mapping (63 ± 8 yrs, 67% male, paroxysmal AF: 35%) with 72 ± 16 GP sites tested to identify 9.7 ± 3.2 GPs. Mapping strategies included ET-GP only (29 patients), mixed ET-GP/AVD-GP (20), and AVD-GP only (5). ET-GPs clustered at the inferior right free wall, right atrial appendage (RAA)-superior vena cava (SVC) junction, RAA-RA interface, anterolateral wall, and posterior intra-atrial septum. Few GP sites were identified on the posterior wall, and none on the cavotricuspid isthmus. AVD-GPs were almost exclusively septal. Notable responses included SVC-induced ectopy, AF initiation, and pulmonary vein ectopy during RA stimulation.

CONCLUSION: The novel Tau20-RETROmapping system enables systematic RA ET-GP mapping. Distinct GP clustering patterns and observed electrophysiological phenomena may enhance understanding of AF mechanisms, particularly non-pulmonary vein triggers.

title: Use of 3D Intracardiac Echocardiography for Concomitant Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation and Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Step by Step Guide.
summary: Intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) has traditionally played a secondary role in atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation and left atrial appendage closure (LAAC), with transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) remaining the standard for appendage imaging. The rise of pulsed field ablation (PFA) has increased interest in adjunctive tools for real-time contact assessment, while trials such as OPTION have highlighted the clinical rationale for combining AF ablation with LAAC in a single procedure. This article describes a step-by-step procedural workflow for concomitant ablation and LAAC using 4D ICE to guide transseptal access, PFA catheter contact, and LAAC device sizing and deployment. Practical troubleshooting strategies for septal crossing and appendage visualization are also discussed.

title: Impact of Real-Time Tissue Proximity Indicator Visualization and Pulsed Field Tag Coloring on Lesion Delivery and Procedural Workflow During Atrial Fibrillation Ablation Using the VARIPULSE Catheter.
summary:
INTRODUCTION: The updated VARIPULSE™ software (V8.1.1.944) introduces a real-time tissue proximity indicator, enhanced VISITAG™ differentiation of complete versus incomplete applications, and grid-based color coding for lesion assessment during pulsed field ablation (PFA). Its impact on procedural workflow and lesion delivery remains insufficiently defined.

METHODS AND RESULTS: We compared 55 pulmonary vein isolation procedures performed with the updated software and 91 procedures performed with the previous version (V8.1.0.325) in 146 consecutive patients with atrial fibrillation. The updated software was associated with a higher number of PFA applications per procedure (19.76 ± 4.10 vs. 17.74 ± 3.90; p < 0.001), with more applications across all pulmonary veins, without increases in fluoroscopy time, radiation dose, or procedure duration (54.06 ± 14.99 vs. 56.64 ± 17.23 min; p = 0.046). Procedure time decreased further after an initial learning curve of 30 cases. First-pass isolation of all pulmonary veins was achieved in 83.6% versus 78.0% of procedures (p = 0.41).

CONCLUSION: These findings suggest modified, proximity-guided lesion delivery without a relevant workflow penalty.

title: Safety and Efficacy of Linear Ablation for Peri-Mitral Annular Atrial Flutter Using the Pentaspline Pulse Field Ablation Catheter.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Despite widespread use of the pentaspline pulse field ablation (PFA) catheter to treat atrial fibrillation, there is limited data supporting its feasibility, safety, and effectiveness in creating linear lesions to treat peri-mitral atrial flutter (AFL).

OBJECTIVE: To assess the safety and efficacy of using the pentaspline PFA catheter to treat peri-mitral AFL.

METHODS: We performed a single-center retrospective review of consecutive patients receiving catheter ablation using the pentaspline PFA catheter to treat peri-mitral macroreentrant AFL.

RESULTS: A total of 80 patients underwent catheter ablation for clinical peri-mitral AFL. Ablation was guided by electroanatomic mapping in all patients. AFL was treated with a lateral mitral line in 38 patients (47.5%), an anteroseptal mitral line in 31 patients (38.8%), a septal mitral line in 6 patients (7.5%), and an anterolateral mitral line in 5 patients (6.3%). Acute procedural success was achieved in 70 patients (87.5%) using the pentaspline catheter; the remaining 10 patients (12.5%) required additional radiofrequency ablation to achieve procedural success. Acute complications occurred in 4 (5.0%) patients: 2 (2.5%) patients sustained electrical isolation of the left atrial appendage, 1 (1.3%) had transient hematuria, and 1 (1.3%) had pericarditis. After a median follow-up of 322 days (IQR 192-432), 42 patients (52.5%) had recurrent AFL. Of these patients, 26 patients underwent a repeat ablation procedure-all demonstrated electrical breakthrough across the prior mitral line.

CONCLUSIONS: While the pentaspline catheter can achieve acute procedural success when treating peri-mitral AFL with linear ablation of the mitral annulus, the long-term efficacy of this treatment strategy is modest.

title: Impact of Selected Cardiac Disorders on Retinal Microcirculation and Choroidal Thickness Assessed by Optical Coherence Tomography and OCT Angiography: A Narrative Review.
summary: Aim: To summarise the impact of cardiovascular diseases on retinal and choroidal microcirculation assessed by optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography (OCTA) in patients with heart failure, myocardial infarction and atrial fibrillation, and to evaluate whether potential microvascular changes detected by OCTA depend on haemodynamic status or treatment. Methods: Published original studies investigating retinal microcirculation using OCTA and choroidal thickness using OCT in patients with selected cardiovascular diseases were reviewed. The analysed OCTA parameters included vessel density in the superficial and deep capillary plexuses, radial peripapillary capillaries, and macular regions, as well as the foveal avascular zone. Subfoveal and central choroidal thickness measurements were considered separately. Associations with cardiac function, haemodynamic status, and treatment-related changes were also reviewed. Results: In patients with heart failure, reduced retinal vessel density was frequently observed. Some studies reported associations between New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class, left ventricular ejection fraction, and retinal microvascular changes. Reduced choroidal thickness was reported in several heart failure studies. In patients with acute decompensated heart failure, perfusion parameters improved following clinical recompensation. Findings in patients with myocardial infarction were inconsistent: while some studies reported no significant differences in retinal vessel density or foveal avascular zone measurements, others demonstrated reduced microvascular density. In patients with atrial fibrillation, decreased flow density in the superficial capillary plexus was reported. Selected studies also demonstrated improvements in certain retinal microvascular parameters and choroidal thickness following interventional procedures. Recent studies described FAZ enlargement and choroidal thinning in HFpEF, and potential associations of deep parafoveal vessel density and choroidal thickness with coronary risk scores in NSTEMI. Conclusions: Current evidence suggests that cardiovascular diseases may be associated with retinal microvascular alterations detectable by OCTA. The most consistent findings concern heart failure and atrial fibrillation, whereas results in patients with myocardial infarction remain inconclusive. OCTA may represent a promising non-invasive tool for investigating microvascular changes associated with cardiovascular disease and exploring treatment-associated microvascular changes; diagnostic and prognostic applications require prospective validation.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Stellate Ganglion Block for Drug-Refractory Electrical Storm After Percutaneous Coronary Intervention for Acute Anterior Myocardial Infarction: A Case Report.
summary: Background/Objectives: Electrical storm (ES) may complicate acute myocardial infarction (AMI). We describe stellate ganglion block (SGB) as an individualized adjunct for refractory ventricular arrhythmias after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Case Presentation: A 68-year-old man with anterior AMI underwent PCI with intra-aortic balloon pump support. From post-PCI day 3, recurrent ventricular tachycardia (VT)/ventricular fibrillation (VF) required 18 cardioversion/defibrillation treatments despite multidrug antiarrhythmic therapy. Monitoring and serial cardiac enzyme measurements showed no clear evidence of recurrent ischemia. Catheter ablation was not pursued because of hemodynamic instability and the family's refusal of further invasive intervention. Ultrasound-guided sequential bilateral SGB was performed daily on 18-20 January 2026, using lidocaine 30 mg and dexmedetomidine 4 μg per side. Results: One brief, self-terminating VT episode followed the first block; no further VT/VF was recorded after the three-day course. Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) increased from 38.1% on 14 January to 45.4% on 19 January, before the third block on 20 January. He was discharged on 21 January. An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was recommended but declined. At telephone follow-up approximately 8 weeks after discharge, he reported no arrhythmic events; at approximately 8 months, he reported independent daily activities. Subsequent cardiac assessments occurred elsewhere; repeat imaging and ambulatory electrocardiographic results were unavailable. Conclusions: SGB was tolerated and temporally associated with arrhythmia suppression in this patient. Concomitant treatment and myocardial recovery may have contributed. A single case cannot establish efficacy, safety, bilateral superiority, or an optimal regimen.

title: Epicardial Adipose Tissue as a Modifiable Cardiometabolic Target: The Role of Nutrition and Physical Exercise-A Narrative Review.
summary: Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) is an active endocrine and paracrine organ involved in coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation (AF), and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Beyond its role as a risk marker, EAT is increasingly investigated as a potentially modifiable target, and exploratory, low-certainty evidence suggests that its response to intervention is only partly explained by weight loss. This narrative review addresses two core themes: the pathophysiology of EAT as a distinct, regionally heterogeneous adipose organ; and the effects of nutrition and physical exercise-particularly the Mediterranean diet, caloric restriction, structured training, and bariatric surgery-on EAT quantity and inflammatory quality. Pharmacological data are summarized only as a complementary comparator. Multimodality imaging-echocardiography, cardiac computed tomography (cCT), and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR)-is discussed as the means by which EAT is measured, and minimum standards for its assessment are proposed. Finally, we outline a hypothesis-generating framework for incorporating EAT assessment into lifestyle-based cardiovascular prevention. This framework has not been validated, and whether reducing EAT improves cardiovascular outcomes independently of weight loss and other risk factors remains unknown; EAT should currently be regarded as a modifiable biomarker rather than an established therapeutic target.

title: TinyML-Based Photoplethysmography (PPG) Analysis for Atrial Fibrillation Detection.
summary: This paper proposes an atrial fibrillation detection algorithm using PPG signals and presents a method to port it to edge devices such as the nRF52840. To classify the PPG signals, simple CNN-based, Autoencoder-based, and Transformer-based Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) were implemented and comparatively analyzed using the MIMIC PERform AF dataset. As a result, the Transformer-based algorithm exhibited the best performance with an average accuracy of 98.66%. While post-training quantization (PTQ) of the Transformer-based algorithm caused the average accuracy to degrade to 95.23%, applying Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) prevented this performance drop. Because some layers of the Transformer are not supported in TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (TFLite Micro), they were modified, and the Multi-Head Attention was approximated using a CNN-based network for porting to the edge device, resulting in a final model size of 107 KB. The ported network demonstrated excellent performance, maintaining an average accuracy of 98.09%.

title: Sudden cardiac death prevention in contemporary cardiovascular care: the role of the wearable cardioverter-defibrillator and coordinated reassessment.
summary: Successful cardiovascular treatment does not necessarily eliminate sudden cardiac death (SCD) risk. After myocardial infarction, newly diagnosed heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, or some other potentially high-risk conditions, clinicians must decide how to protect patients while treatment is optimized and the need for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is reassessed.This review examines the evidence for the wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD) and its relevance to contemporary cardiovascular care. Randomized and observational studies inform patient selection, sustained wear, and reassessment, but appropriate device interventions should be distinguished from demonstrated mortality benefit. Contemporary medical therapy can reduce SCD risk and improve ventricular function, although optimization takes time and residual risk remains. Catheter ablation may address ventricular arrhythmia burden and residual substrate but does not replace an indicated ICD. Japanese studies suggest that some eligible patients may not receive a discussion regarding device-based protection.We propose protected risk reassessment: temporary protection when appropriate, treatment optimization, and a planned decision about subsequent device therapy. An identified SCD prevention doctor or team should coordinate this pathway. The role is defined primarily by commitment to prevention and responsibility for continuity of care, supported by ongoing education and access to specialist expertise, rather than by subspecialty or affiliation alone.The aim is to connect risk recognition with an informed treatment plan and ensure that each patient reaches reassessment. Substrate-directed ventricular tachycardia treatment, risk markers beyond LVEF, and questions after structural interventions provide additional context, but do not substitute for appropriate device protection. The optimal duration of temporary protection remains a research priority.Graphical Abstract Cardiovascular treatment may improve symptoms and hemodynamics without eliminating residual arrhythmic risk. Temporary protection with a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD), optimization of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), assessment of the arrhythmogenic substrate, and ventricular arrhythmia treatment may inform individualized reassessment. Subsequent ICD decisions require risk assessment, patient preferences, and planned follow-up. The proposed SCD prevention doctor/team coordinates this process; the framework does not itself establish additional device indications or outcome benefits.

title: Fluoropyrimidine-Associated Cardiotoxicity: Coronary Vasospasm, Rechallenge Strategies, and Vasodilator Prophylaxis.
summary: Fluoropyrimidines, principally 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) and capecitabine, remain foundational agents in the treatment of gastrointestinal, breast, and head and neck malignancies, but they are also among the most clinically important non-anthracycline causes of cancer therapy-related cardiovascular toxicity. Clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic electrocardiographic abnormalities and biomarker elevation to angina, coronary vasospasm, myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, heart failure, Takotsubo syndrome, and sudden cardiac death. Although coronary vasospasm remains the most recognized mechanism, contemporary evidence supports a multifactorial pathophysiology involving endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, direct myocardial injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, thrombosis, and microvascular dysfunction. The reported incidence varies widely because of differences in definitions, surveillance intensity, cancer populations, and fluoropyrimidine schedules. Management begins with immediate discontinuation of fluoropyrimidine and evaluation for acute coronary syndrome or other cardiac emergencies. A major unresolved question is whether fluoropyrimidine therapy can be safely resumed after cardiotoxicity. Older reports suggested high recurrence rates with rechallenge, whereas more recent cardio-oncology-guided series suggest that selected patients may successfully continue treatment using vasodilator prophylaxis, regimen modification, and close monitoring. This narrative review summarizes the epidemiology, mechanisms, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, acute management, rechallenge strategies, and alternatives to fluoropyrimidines when re-exposure is unsafe.

title: Current practices in the investigation of sudden cardiac death in Southeastern Europe countries: results of a multinational survey
Avoiding Resternotomy: Minimally Invasive Redo Mitral Valve Surgery in a Two-Center Series.
summary: Background/Objectives: Mitral surgery after previous cardiac operations requires an approach adapted to prior procedures and current valve pathology. We describe operative strategies and early outcomes of minimally invasive redo mitral valve surgery in a two-center series. Methods: We reviewed 45 consecutive patients treated through right minithoracotomy at two centers between January 2020 and July 2026. Operative characteristics, complications, early echocardiography, and available follow-up were assessed. This was a descriptive analysis without a sternotomy control group. Early mortality was defined as death during the index hospitalization. Echocardiographic outcomes were summarized separately for early and classifiable follow-up examinations; patients without evaluable imaging were not included in those denominators. Results: Mean age was 65.0 ± 12.4 years; 20 patients (44.4%) were women. Repair was performed in 15 (33.3%) and replacement in 30 (66.7%). Median cardiopulmonary bypass time was 152 min. Aortic cross-clamping was used in 20 patients (44.4%) and hypothermic ventricular fibrillation in 25 (55.6%). No conversion to sternotomy occurred. Early echocardiography was satisfactory in 43/44 (97.7%). Stroke occurred in 2/45 (4.4%), rethoracotomy in 3/45 (6.7%), pacemaker implantation in 3/45 (6.7%), and in-hospital death in 3/45 (6.7%). Good valve function was documented in 29/33 patients with classifiable follow-up (87.9%). Conclusions: Redo mitral repair and replacement through right minithoracotomy were completed without sternotomy conversion. These descriptive results support feasibility in experienced centers; larger comparative studies are needed.

title: Atrial Leadless Pacing in Combination with Existing ICD Systems in Long QT Syndrome.
summary: Long QT syndrome is an inherited or acquired condition characterized by prolonged ventricular repolarization and is characterized by a propensity for life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias. Management often incorporates beta blockers, which have the greatest effect on reducing arrhythmic risk, and implantable cardiac defibrillator (ICD) implantation. Subcutaneous ICDs provide effective defibrillation therapy while avoiding intravascular leads and are an attractive option for patients at high risk of infection or thrombosis, or for younger patients to reduce intravascular lead dwell time. Subcutaneous ICDs provide defibrillation therapy but do not offer pacing and antitachycardia pacing. Leadless pacemakers are often favored for similar reasons, and combined use with ICDs introduces challenges, including device interaction. We report 2 cases of interaction between ICD sensing and atrial leadless pacemakers in long QT syndrome, including a case of S-ICD oversensing, not yet described in the literature, and a comparative case in a transvenous system.

title: Idiopathic Ventricular Fibrillation: Long-Term Outcomes.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation (IVF) is diagnosed in survivors of sudden cardiac arrest when no underlying cause is identified. Predicting prognosis in patients with IVF remains challenging. In this case series, we describe 3 patients with IVF to explore the clinical course of IVF.

CASE SUMMARY: Patient 1 experienced multiple recurrences within the first years following the index event. Patient 2 remained free of arrhythmic events over 30 years and ultimately chose implantable cardioverter-defibrillator explantation. Patient 3 initially appeared to follow a similarly benign course, but experienced a late recurrence 23 years after the index event.

DISCUSSION: We illustrated the course of IVF, ranging from decades without events to frequent recurrences, even after decades without events. Distinct subgroups may exist; however, further research is necessary to identify them.

TAKE-HOME MESSAGES: These cases show the heterogeneity and unpredictability of long-term outcomes in patients with IVF. In the absence of reliable predictors, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator therapy remains essential in patients with IVF.

title: Myocardial Scar-Detected Cardiac Magnetic Resonance on Left Bundle-Branch Area Pacing Outcomes: A Systematic Review.
summary:
BACKGROUND: The implantation of conduction system pacing (CSP), in particular left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP), involves deep septal lead deployment 1.5 cm distal to the His bundle to achieve subendocardial capture of the left bundle branch; hence, myocardial scar is theoretically a critical determinant of both procedural success and subsequent CRT response. This review aimed to evaluate the impact of myocardial scar assessed by cardiac magnetic resonance late gadolinium enhancement (CMR-LGE) on LBBAP outcomes.

METHODS: Three electronic databases (Scopus, PubMed, and ScienceDirect) were searched for eligible studies from database inception until June, 12 2026. When at least two studies reported comparable quantitative outcomes, random-effects meta-analysis was performed using RStudio.

RESULTS: Eight studies (n = 581 patients) met the eligibility criteria. Qualitatively, the presence of myocardial scar attenuates lead placement and electrical resynchronization, with smaller reductions in left ventricular activation and dyssynchrony, wider paced QRS duration, and more loss of conduction-system capture. Higher scar burden was associated with attenuated reverse remodeling (LVEF improvement, LVESV reduction, and LVEDD reduction). Higher scar burden was also associated with a higher risk of heart failure hospitalization, ventricular arrhythmia, and all-cause mortality. Quantitatively, CRT responders had lower baseline global LGE burden (MD -6.27%; 95% CI -10.84 to -1.70; p = 0.0072) and septal LGE burden (MD -7.94%; 95% CI -11.87 to -4.00; p < 0.0001) than non-responders.

CONCLUSION: Myocardial scar may determine LBBAP outcomes, with the septal scar emerging as the most consistent predictor of worse outcomes. This qualitative early analysis supports pre-procedural LGE-CMR in selected LBBAP patients.

title: From Acute Infectious Myocarditis to Chronic Inflammatory Cardiomyopathy: Pathophysiological Mechanisms, Key Investigations, and Current Treatment Strategies.
summary: Acute infectious myocarditis is an inflammatory disease of the myocardium caused by a broad range of infectious agents, including viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, helminths, and spirochetes. Its clinical presentation is highly variable, ranging from asymptomatic or mild self-limiting disease to fulminant heart failure, life-threatening arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, and sudden cardiac death. Although many patients recover completely, persistent myocardial inflammation, incomplete pathogen clearance, immune-mediated injury, and myocardial fibrosis may lead to adverse ventricular remodelling, persistent ventricular dysfunction, and progression to chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy or dilated cardiomyopathy. The pathophysiology reflects a complex interaction between direct pathogen-mediated myocardial injury and innate and adaptive immune responses, with the balance between effective pathogen clearance and excessive inflammation being a major determinant of outcome. Diagnosis remains challenging because clinical manifestations and conventional investigations are often nonspecific. A multimodal approach incorporating electrocardiography, cardiac biomarkers, echocardiography, cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), microbiological and molecular investigations, and, in selected patients, endomyocardial biopsy is essential for diagnosis and risk stratification. CMR is particularly valuable for identifying myocardial edema, inflammation, necrosis, and fibrosis, whereas endomyocardial biopsy remains important in selected severe or diagnostically uncertain cases. Treatment is primarily guided by clinical severity and the identified infectious etiology. Management includes supportive heart failure therapy, arrhythmia control, temporary restriction of physical activity, and mechanical circulatory support in severe or fulminant disease. Targeted antimicrobial therapy is essential when a treatable pathogen is identified, while routine empiric antiviral therapy or immunosuppression is not currently supported for most presumed viral myocarditis. Emerging approaches involving molecular diagnostics, immunological profiling, novel biomarkers, targeted modulation of inflammatory pathways, and personalized therapies may improve diagnosis and outcomes. This review summarizes current evidence on the etiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, treatment, and progression from infectious myocarditis to chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy.

title: The Lancet Sudden Cardiac Death Commission: joining multi-disciplinary forces to combat sudden cardiac death.
Chronic Q fever prosthetic valve endocarditis with a retained pacemaker: multidisciplinary and infection prevention considerations.
summary: Introduction. Chronic Q fever, caused by Coxiella burnetii, is an important cause of culture-negative infective endocarditis particularly in patients with congenital valvular disease or prosthetic valves. Clinical presentation is often insidious and diagnosis is challenging, relying predominantly on serology and molecular diagnostics. Case presentation. A man in his 60s with a bioprosthetic aortic valve for prior bicuspid aortic valve disease and a permanent pacemaker was referred after an incidental echocardiographic abnormality. He reported several years of non-specific symptoms but was afebrile at presentation and multiple blood cultures yielded no clinically significant pathogen. Imaging demonstrated severe paravalvular regurgitation and dehiscence of the prosthetic aortic valve, prompting redo aortic valve and aortic root replacement. Cultures of the excised valve remained negative, while broad-range 16S rRNA PCR identified C. burnetii. Serology supported a diagnosis of Q fever endocarditis, with a phase I IgG titre of 1:10,240. Following diagnosis, the specialist Q fever multidisciplinary team recommended pacemaker retention following a risk-benefit assessment, alongside 24 months of doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine, with a minimum of 18 months. At 4-month follow-up, antibody titres remained unchanged, while C-reactive protein had normalized. Conclusion. This case illustrates the difficulty of diagnosing C. burnetii prosthetic valve endocarditis in the absence of classical clinical features. The postoperative diagnosis also raised challenges regarding pacemaker retention and potential occupational exposure during surgery, emphasizing the importance of detailed occupational history-taking and early consideration of Q fever in culture-negative endocarditis.

title: Role of Cardiac Magnetic Resonance in Predicting Response to Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Although cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) is now a standard treatment for many patients with heart failure and electrical dyssynchrony. Response to CRT represents a major daily challenge in clinical practice. This meta-analysis aimed to synthesize and analyze the available evidence to determine whether pre-implant CMR markers can reliably differentiate CRT responders from non-responders.

METHODS: A systematic search was conducted through December 2025. We included studies involving adults undergoing CRT who had undergone CMR before implantation and who reported outcomes separately for responders and non-responders. Quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Primary outcomes included scar burden and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE). Continuous data were pooled as mean difference (MD), while dichotomous data were pooled as odds ratios (OR) with their corresponding 95% confidence interval (95% CI).

RESULTS: Thirteen cohort studies were included, providing data on 543 responders and 347 non-responders. Responders had markedly lower scar burden than non-responders. The pooled MD indicated that responders had, on average, 12.86% less scar tissue. Patients who responded to CRT were significantly less likely to exhibit LGE, with no heterogeneity. For secondary outcomes, responders and non-responders had similar baseline LVESV, LVEDV, and LVEF.

CONCLUSION: This meta-analysis demonstrates that key CMR markers, particularly scar burden and LGE, are strongly associated with CRT response, while volumetric and functional parameters further support their predictive value. Despite heterogeneity across studies, the overall findings suggest that pre-implant CMR can meaningfully help identify patients more likely to benefit from CRT.

title: Impact of Cardiac CT-Defined True Septal Right Ventricular Lead Position on Electrical and Structural Remodeling After Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy With Defibrillator Implantation.
summary:
INTRODUCTION: The impact of true right ventricular (RV) septal lead positioning on response to cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) remains controversial. We investigated the association between cardiac computed tomography (CT)-defined RV defibrillator lead position and CRT response.

METHODS: This retrospective study included 105 patients who underwent CRT-defibrillator (CRT-D) implantation and post-implantation cardiac CT to assess RV lead position. All patients had documented biventricular pacing ≥ 90% at 6 months. Based on CT findings, patients were classified into a true septal RV lead group (n = 56) and a non-septal group (n = 49). Changes in QRS duration and echocardiographic parameters at 6 months and long-term clinical outcomes were compared between the groups. CRT response was defined as a ≥ 15% reduction in left ventricular end-systolic volume (LVESV) at 6 months.

RESULTS: Post-implantation QRS duration was significantly shorter in the septal group than in the non-septal group (136.2 ± 15.8 vs. 157.4 ± 21.8 ms, p < 0.001). At 6 months, the septal group showed greater improvements in left ventricular ejection fraction (Δ8.4 ± 9.7% vs. 3.8 ± 8.5%, p = 0.011) and LVESV (Δ-31.8 ± 39.2 vs. -11.9 ± 39.1 mL, p = 0.013), with a higher CRT response rate (73.2% vs. 42.9%, p = 0.003). Multivariable analysis demonstrated that true septal RV lead positioning was independently associated with CRT response (odds ratio, 3.33; 95% confidence interval, 1.13-9.78; p = 0.029). No significant between-group differences were observed in mortality or heart failure hospitalization.

CONCLUSIONS: Cardiac CT-defined true septal RV lead positioning was associated with greater electrical resynchronization and enhanced LV reverse remodeling after CRT-D implantation. Anatomical RV lead position may represent an important modifiable determinant of CRT response.

title: Atrial Pacing Capability of a Single-Lead Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator Incorporating an Atrial Floating Dipole.
summary:
INTRODUCTION: The single-lead DX implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) combines the advantages of a conventional single-lead ICD with atrial sensing capability provided by an integrated atrial floating dipole. While atrial sensing performance has been extensively documented, the ability of the floating atrial dipole to achieve atrial capture has not previously been investigated.

METHODS AND RESULTS: Consecutive patients undergoing de novo implantation or generator replacement of a single-lead DX ICD system at two Italian centers were prospectively enrolled. Acute atrial pacing was assessed using three configurations: bipolar pacing and two unipolar configurations employing either the proximal or distal atrial electrode. Atrial capture, pacing threshold (PT), impedance, and phrenic nerve stimulation were evaluated at pulse widths of 0.4 and 1.0 ms. Twenty-five patients (92% male; mean age 66.2 ± 10.1 years) were included. Acute atrial capture was achieved in 22 patients (88%) with bipolar pacing, compared with 18 (72%) and 17 (68%) using proximal and distal unipolar pacing, respectively (p = 0.122). Bipolar pacing yielded significantly lower PTs than unipolar configurations at both pulse widths (p < 0.020). Median atrial sensing amplitude measured after connection to the ICD generator was 3.9 mV (2.8-5.1).

CONCLUSION: Atrial capture through the floating atrial dipole of a single-lead DX ICD system is feasible in the majority of patients, with bipolar pacing providing the highest capture rate and the lowest PTs. These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence supporting further development of single-lead dual-chamber sensing and pacing strategies using the DX platform.

title: Safety and feasibility of large-bore internal jugular vein access for leadless pacemaker implantation: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Leadless pacemaker (LP) implantation requires a large-bore (up to 27-French) delivery sheath. The femoral vein is the standard access route; however, it carries the risk of major bleeding and may be precluded by venous occlusion. The internal jugular vein (IJV) provides an alternative trajectory. Consolidated data on its vascular safety and procedural feasibility are lacking.

METHODS: We searched PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science through December 2025 for studies evaluating IJV-guided LP implantation. Pooled incidence rates and risk ratios (RR) for comparative cohorts were estimated using a random-effects model.

RESULTS: Eleven observational studies were included after outcome-specific removal of overlapping participants. The descriptive IJV cohorts showed high reported procedural success, but definitions and denominators varied across outcomes. In two non-randomized comparative cohorts, no major vascular access-site events were reported in the IJV arms (0/132) and 17 were reported in the femoral arms (17/124). These unadjusted comparisons were at serious-to-critical risk of bias because of historical controls, baseline imbalances, differential ultrasound use, and non-standardized event ascertainment.

CONCLUSION: IJV access appears technically feasible for leadless pacemaker implantation in selected adult and pediatric patients. Evidence is insufficient to determine whether it reduces vascular or overall major complications compared with femoral access. Prospective multicenter studies with standardized outcome definitions, protocolized vascular surveillance, and contemporaneous comparators are required.

title: Dual-Chamber Leadless Pacemaker Implantation Via a Left-Sided Inferior Vena Cava After Pacemaker Extraction.
summary:
BACKGROUND: A left-sided inferior vena cava (IVC) may complicate transfemoral leadless pacemaker implantation.

CASE SUMMARY: A 71-year-old man with complete atrioventricular block required reimplantation after extraction for recurrent pacemaker infection. Bilateral subclavian venous occlusion favored leadless pacing. Computed tomography identified a left-sided IVC. A recent left femoral neck fracture precluded left femoral access. Right femoral venography confirmed the anomalous course, which was substantially straightened by a 27-F delivery sheath. Repositioning the sheath tip at the IVC-right atrial junction enabled successful ventricular and atrial AVEIR implantation. Dual-chamber pacing and sensing with dual response to sensing (DDD) pacing remained stable at 1 month.

DISCUSSION: Sheath insertion altered the venous geometry, while sheath-tip repositioning facilitated delivery of both devices.

TAKE-HOME MESSAGES: Preprocedural imaging guides access planning. Reassessment of venous geometry after large-bore sheath insertion and optimization of sheath-tip positioning may facilitate dual-chamber leadless pacing through a left-sided IVC.

title: Cardiac sarcoidosis uncovered after pacemaker implantation.
Device - Based Autonomic Modulation in Arrhythmia and Beyond.
summary:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Autonomic imbalance contributes to the initiation and maintenance of cardiac arrhythmias and represents an emerging therapeutic target. This review summarizes the current evidence for device-based and targeted autonomic neuromodulation and evaluates its potential across arrhythmias and cardiovascular disease.

RECENT FINDINGS: Preclinical and clinical studies of vagus nerve stimulation, ganglionated plexus ablation, renal and cardiac sympathetic denervation and baroreflex activation therapy demonstrate beneficial effects on autonomic tone, electrophysiological remodeling, inflammation and arrhythmic burden. Emerging evidence also supports applications beyond arrhythmias, including heart failure and systemic inflammatory disease. Although neuromodulation shows promising therapeutic potential, clinical efficacy remains heterogeneous, with important uncertainties regarding optimal targets, stimulation parameters, patient selection, and treatment monitoring. Future research should prioritize standardized protocols, validated biomarkers, phenotype-specific strategies, and closed-loop approaches.

title: Cardiovascular Assessment of the Athlete's Heart: From Electrocardiography and Multimodality Imaging to Genetic Testing and Shared Decision-Making.
summary: Sustained athletic training induces structural, functional, and electrical cardiac remodeling, collectively termed the "athlete's heart," which may phenotypically overlap with inherited and acquired cardiomyopathies. Distinguishing benign exercise-induced remodeling from occult heart disease is critical, since diagnostic error in either direction carries meaningful consequences, ranging from unwarranted sports disqualification to failure to identify athletes at risk of exercise-related sudden cardiac death. In this narrative review, based on a PubMed/MEDLINE search of the literature published between 2015 and 2026, we summarize the contemporary cardiovascular assessment of athletes, including electrocardiography, echocardiography with speckle-tracking and myocardial work, exercise testing, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), cardiac computed tomography, nuclear imaging, genetic testing, detraining, sex-specific considerations, and artificial intelligence (AI). Electrocardiography interpreted according to the International Criteria, echocardiography and, when indicated, CMR form the core of the evaluation, whereas the other tools are complementary and reserved for selected clinical questions. Many proposed numerical cut-offs derive from single cohorts and are not interchangeable across vendors, protocols, sexes, ethnicities, and sporting disciplines, and some athletes remain indeterminate despite comprehensive evaluation. We propose a pragmatic, non-validated stepwise framework that keeps diagnostic classification, arrhythmic risk assessment, and sports eligibility distinct and emphasizes multidisciplinary shared decision-making.

title: Broken heart, twisted rhythm: a case report of percutaneous stellate ganglion block for Torsades de Pointes in Takotsubo stress cardiomyopathy.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TCM) is characterized by transient apical ballooning of the left ventricle (LV) and accounts for 1%-3% of cases of suspected acute coronary syndrome. QT interval (QT) prolongation occurs in most patients with TCM and peaks on approximately day three but may persist for weeks. During this period, patients are at risk of Torsades de Pointes (TdP), which is reported in 2%-4% of cases of TCM. Proposed mechanisms for QT prolongation include catecholamine excess, ion channel dysfunction, and repolarization dispersion from myocardial oedema. Prolonged action potential duration and delayed phase-3 repolarization predispose to early after depolarizations (EADs) and subsequent TdP.

CASE SUMMARY: An 80-year-old woman undergoing treatment of acute myeloid leukaemia suffered a TdP-related cardiac arrest. An electrocardiogram demonstrated diffuse T-wave inversion and a corrected QT of 530 ms. Echocardiography showed severe hypokinesis of the apical third of the LV-consistent with TCM. Coronary disease was excluded. Her QTc peaked at 635 ms and she had recurrent TdP arrests despite beta-blockade. She finally underwent a percutaneous stellate ganglion block (PSGB) and over the following weeks, her heart rate and QTc normalized without further recurrence of TdP.

DISCUSSION: Beta-blockers are commonly used in TCM, although evidence for arrhythmia prevention is limited and haemodynamic compromise may limit use. PSGB targets the left cervico-thoracic sympathetic chain, temporarily reducing catecholaminergic outflow. The resulting sympatholysis slows heart rate, shortens the QTc interval, and suppresses EADs-reducing TdP risk. PSGB has shown effectiveness in refractory ventricular tachycardia from different aetiologies; however, its use specifically in TCM-related TdP has rarely been reported.

title: Cardiac amyloidosis: contemporary diagnosis and management with illustrative cases of ATTR and AL subtypes.
summary:
INTRODUCTION: Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an increasingly recognized, treatable cause of heart failure. Prompt distinction between transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) and light-chain cardiac amyloidosis (AL-CA) is critical because delayed AL diagnosis can be fatal.

AREAS COVERED: This narrative review examines epidemiology, mechanisms, multimodality imaging, diagnostic algorithms, and established and emerging therapies. Literature was identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane Library searches and reference screening; the original search dates require author confirmation. Emphasis is placed on immediate serum free light-chain and serum/urine immunofixation testing, nonbiopsy ATTR diagnosis in eligible patients, and TTR sequencing after ATTR confirmation. Three clinical cases illustrate diagnostic and therapeutic challenges.

EXPERT OPINION: Earlier diagnosis, urgent exclusion of AL-CA, universal TTR genetic testing, and multisystem evaluation of hereditary ATTR are essential. Multidisciplinary, phenotype-guided care and validated treatment-response measures will be increasingly important as therapies expand.

title: [Right ventricular abnormalities and familial sudden cardiac death: incidental finding or arrhythmogenic substrate?].
summary: We report the case of a 42-year-old man referred to our center following the sudden cardiac death of his brother. The ECG and transthoracic echocardiography were apparently within normal limits. Twenty-four-hour Holter ECG monitoring revealed rare polymorphic ventricular ectopic beats. In light of the family history and arrhythmic findings, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was performed, showing right ventricular dilation in the absence of fibrosis or fibro-fatty infiltration. Subsequent genetic testing identified a pathogenic variant in the KCNQ1 gene, associated with type 1 long QT syndrome. This case highlights the pivotal role of thorough family history assessment and genetic analysis in arrhythmic risk stratification among screened patients, even in the presence of inconclusive structural findings. Furthermore, it emphasizes the potential value of systematically performing autopsies, including molecular ones, on victims of sudden death and prompts reflection on the genotype-phenotype relationship of variants in potassium channel-encoding genes, beyond the established spectrum of inherited channelopathies.

title: ECPR-to-Heart Transplant in a Young Woman With PPA2-Associated Metabolic Cardiomyopathy Presenting as Inferolateral STEMI.
summary:
BACKGROUND: PPA2-related mitochondrial cardiomyopathy is a rare, autosomal recessive disorder associated with rapidly progressive dilated cardiomyopathy, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. Heightened sensitivity to alcohol has been reported in some affected individuals. Heart transplantation in affected patients is rarely reported.

CASE SUMMARY: A 21-year-old woman with no prior history presented with chest pain, dyspnea, abdominal pain, and vomiting after alcohol intake. Electrocardiogram showed inferior and lateral ST-segment elevation. She developed pulseless electrical activity arrest en route to coronary angiography and underwent extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Coronary angiography was normal. Echocardiography revealed severe biventricular dysfunction (left ventricular ejection fraction <20%). Despite Impella 5.5 support, no recovery occurred. Whole-genome sequencing identified pathogenic and likely pathogenic PPA2 variants, confirming PPA2-related mitochondrial cardiomyopathy. She underwent successful orthotopic heart transplantation.

DISCUSSION: This case highlights fulminant cardiogenic shock due to PPA2-related cardiomyopathy. Rapid genomic sequencing established the diagnosis when angiography and endomyocardial biopsy were unrevealing, informed prognosis, and enabled genetic counseling and cascade family testing.

TAKE-HOME MESSAGES: PPA2 cardiomyopathy should be suspected in young patients with arrest, severe ventricular dysfunction, and normal coronaries. Rapid genomic sequencing can be diagnostic and guide management.

title: Clinical, electrocardiographic and echocardiographic features of childhood cardiomyopathy in the United Arab Emirates
summary: BACKGROUND Cardiomyopathy (CMP) is one of the main causes of heart failure in children. Genetic and metabolic etiology are common in regions with high consanguinity. AIM To describe the clinical, electrocardiographic and echocardiographic features of childhood CMP in the United Arab Emirates. METHODS This retrospective cohort study was conducted at a tertiary care hospital in the United Arab Emirates, covering a period from 2020 to 2025. Historical data back to January 2013 were retrieved for survival analysis. All children with CMP were included. Demographic, clinical, electrocardiography, and echocardiography (echo) data were collected. Metabolic and genetic studies were included. RESULTS The study included 200 cases of CMP (60% were female). The cohort comprised 25 ethnic groups, with consanguinity status known for 70 families and positive in 31%. The most common age of presentation was 0-6 months. Syndromic features and neurodevelopmental delays were found in 28% and 33% of the cases, respectively. Long QT syndrome was diagnosed in 9% of the patients. Metabolic screening was positive in 15% of the cohort. The most common abnormalities were conditions associated with high lactate levels (31%), followed by conditions associated with high ammonia levels (15%). Genetic testing was positive in 21.5% of the cohort. The most common genetic abnormality was Noonan’s syndrome, followed by Alström and CHARGE syndromes; the latter, to our knowledge, has not been previously reported. Hypertrophic CMP (HCM) was the most common type (47%), followed by dilated CMP (36.5%), noncompaction CMP (14%), and restrictive CMP (2.5%). Patients with HCM presented significantly earlier and had more associated syndromic features (P < 0.041). There was statistically higher mortality in patients with noncompaction CMP associated with low EF or with HCM (combined) and a higher recovery rate in those with DCM (P < 0.05). The whole cohort mortality rate was 12%, and it was 25% for those with positive genetic testing. The mean (95%CI) of overall survival was 73.8 months. There were significantly lower survival rates in patients with edema. CONCLUSION In this highly consanguineous population, CMP is more prevalent in females and presents mostly in early infancy. The most common type is HCM. Genetic and metabolic disorders are common and are associated with higher mortality rates.

title: When is a PVI "successful"? Characterising OCEAN/ALONE-AF Enrolment Criteria with Continuous Rhythm Monitoring.
summary:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: The OCEAN/ALONE-AF trials demonstrated low stroke risk in patients deemed AF-free 12 months post-ablation using intermittent Holter monitoring. Whether these patients had true AF freedom or had undetected AF remains unknown. We characterised the rhythm phenotype selected by this enrolment strategy.

METHODS: SINGLE-SHOT CHAMPION and COMPARE-CRYO are randomised trials in paroxysmal AF patients undergoing ablation, with implantable cardiac monitors (ICM) used for continuous rhythm monitoring. This post-hoc analysis included patients with no clinical atrial tachyarrhythmia (ATA) recurrence within 12 months and CHA2DS2-VA ≥1. Monte Carlo simulations (n=5,000) using individual-level ICM data replicated the OCEAN/ALONE-AF eligibility criteria (two simulated 48-hour Holter). Misclassification rates and ATA burden were quantified.

RESULTS: Of 411 patients, 232 were eligible (172 cryoballoon ablation, 60 pulsed-field ablation). Simulated intermittent Holter monitoring classified as ATA-free 223 patients (96.1%; 95% simulation interval [SI] 94.4-97.8%); however, 67 patients (30.0% 95% SI 28.8-31.3%) had ATA on ICM. Among these 223 patients, ATA burden was very low (<0.1%) in 20.6%, low (0.1-1.0%) in 8.7%, and moderate (>1.0%) in 0.7%. In an exploratory analysis, misclassification was numerically higher in patients with CHA2DS2-VA≥3 (33.4% vs. 27.4%). Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses.

CONCLUSIONS: Approximately one-third of patients deemed ATA-free by OCEAN/ALONE-AF criteria had undetected ATA recurrence on ICM, with very low ATA burden (<0.1%). These findings suggest that the low stroke rates in OCEAN/ALONE-AF may reflect successful arrhythmia burden suppression rather than complete arrhythmia eradication, with intermittent Holter monitoring serving as a pragmatic surrogate for a low-burden state.
